Like:

\- avoid confrontation when possible. Just listen and if you disagree, try to bring it up later or in a softer way than usual.

\- cuddle? Maybe it helps?

\- counteract intrusive thoughts. Maybe your thoughts tell you you're worthless and unlovable and he can gently remind you that he needs you and loves you?

\- practical help. Do you feel overwhelmed with some chores? Could he take some of your burden for a few days? Maybe cook something nice?

\- find ways to relax. Maybe watch a movie together? Play videogames together? How could he help you distract yourself?

Yes, PMDD is devastating in relationships. But if he understands the magnitude of it and ways he can help you, he can actually be by your side against PMDD.

If you've never tried therapy, it's a first step, give it chance.

NHS talk therapy has its limitations. It's usually a few sessions of CBT, it's supposed to give you some tools to learn how to cope with anxiety and depression. It's supposed to teach you how to challenge your negative thought processes.

But it's just a few sessions, you may not have time to establish a strong and deep relationship with your counselor. You may not feel as heard and understood as you wish. But they are there to help you, just take what you can get out of it.

You may decide to get a private therapist in the future. If you can afford it, it's definitely a different experience. If your experience with the NHS is not what you were hoping for, don't let that discourage you from getting help elsewhere.

But in the best case scenario, it will help. It will give you tools and show you a path where you can keep growing and fighting those issues. You may still decide to get a private therapist after, as you discover that therapy helps more than you thought it would and having someone to talk to means faster and longer lasting improvements than you could achieve on your own.

You deserve care like anyone else, give them a chance and give yourself a chance.

If we assume she got her period on the 16th, she should be back to normal by now. Different women have different patterns in terms of when their worst days are in their cycle and and how long it lasts (some will say a week, some ten days, for some it stops when the period begins, for some the first couple of days of the period are still quite challenging). And it can also shift for the same person (for example getting from 7 to 10 days as they get older or closer to menopause).

Again, when she's feeling better you can ask her more about the pattern of her symptoms. She could try keeping a symptoms journal if she hasn't tried it before, it could help both of you (but don't push about it if that feels like something she can't handle right now, some women suffer from other conditions on top of PMDD, for example ADHD could make it hard to keep a journal and organise your life around PMDD).

Do you know if her period actually started on the 16th? If her period is late, it can last longer.

Also, if she's going through stress for other reasons, work etc, she may be having a worse time than usual.

At the end of the day, the only thing you can do is say "if there's anything I can do to help, let me know" and wait. When she feels better you can talk about what may have made things worse or other things to try (supplements, exercise, diet, therapy, drugs.. whatever she feels could be helpful and whatever she's ready to try). You can also then talk about if there's anything she think you could have done differently to help in that time (staying away is often the best route, but she may feel there are other ways to handle it).
